9 Discussion and Conclusion

We introduced AgentSSL, which formulates semi-supervised learning as agentic program search. Under label scarcity, MLE agents generate SSL programs that beat tuned human baselines in 8 of 12 settings when the best program is known, but neither agents nor human pipelines can reliably pick that program without labels.

We decompose this problem into two core challenges:(1) program discovery, where agents must discover effective SSL programs under limited feedback, and(2) program selection, where a single program must be identified from the discovered candidates without a large labeled validation set.

6 Analysis

question: What does oracle performance measure when assessing program discovery?

results.text: Evaluation. We evaluate these two challenges separately. To assess program discovery, we measure oracle performance, defined as the test performance of the best program in the discovered pool, Q(A∗). This measures the quality of the best discovered solution, independent of our ability to select it.

When the metric is well correlated with test performance, much of the oracle performance is retained; when this alignment is weak, selection performance can degrade substantially. These results suggest that practical program selection is a major bottleneck for AgentSSL.

5 Results

Across datasets and shot settings, AgentSSL discovers programs that are competitive with strong SSL baselines when programs are selected using oracle test performance (Table 1).

question: Under what condition is it better to spend labels on program selection rather than on training?

results.text: We also introducedProgramSelectBench(Appendix C), which makes this selection problem measurable, and our results show that when unsupervised metrics fail, labels spent on selection buy more accuracy than the same labels spent on training.

When unsupervised metrics fail, active model selection offers a promising alternative by using labels for selection. Under a fixed budget, we compare training on all labels with unsupervised selection against splitting labels evenly between training and active selection (Table 3).

For example, on the RETINO (40-shot) noisy validation task, both CODA and ModelSelector get to zero regret with less than 25 labels, but after 40 labels, they suddenly select a program with 30% worse accuracy.

question: Why can metrics based on learned representations fail to tell agent-generated programs apart?

results.text: We provide a comprehensive evaluation of all unsupervised selection metrics on ProgramSelectBench in Appendix C. A limitation of unsupervised selection is that its metrics necessarily encode assumptions about what constitutes a good model. For example, several metrics assess properties of learned representations.

First, we find that unsupervised metrics enable effective selection when underlying assumptions hold. Second, when unsupervised metrics fail, actively allocating labels to program selection can outperform allocating them to training.

Unsupervised MetricsInspired by prior work [ 59], we use an ensemble of different unsupervised metrics as feedback for the agentic search. Since different unsupervised metrics capture different properties of the learned representations and predictions, an ensemble should be able to balance these biases.
